rv.q: Jackson's Lear is a towering achievement that confirms her status as one of the greatest living actresses.
So deeply does Jackson adopt the king's sense of entitlement, perhaps, that she barely stoops to emotional display at all.
But this “Lear” mostly gains its power from the stimulating interrelationships etched by the women in the cast, playing roles of either gender.
But although Jackson fails to wring tears, let alone blood, from this production, the sheer intelligence of her performance makes it memorable.
A radical, enigmatic and uneven production that nonetheless showcases one of the great actresses of the stage
Still, for all its weaknesses, the staging is never dull. And watching Jackson is a reward in itself.
But much of what surrounds her in this glittery, haphazard production seems to be working overtime to divert attention from that performance.
But if this revival represents a step forward for Gold’s career, it is a step backward for Shakespeare’s play, which has lost much of its excruciating pathos in the directorial hubbub.
See it now for Jackson, towering even in Lear's infirmity, and for its other occasional felicities, but know that it's still a slog.
Confoundingly muddled evening...no one is going to go near this thorny brute of a play there again anytime soon.
Blurry and superficial, the shape of power without its impact, the production that is little more than Lear’s shadow.
Given a wickedly sly look by scenic designer Miriam Buether (all that Trump Tower gold can’t be unintentional), this Lear is a knock-out.

Sam Gold's outstanding production of Lear now at New York's Cort Theatre
Its only fault, and it was a significantly intrusive one for this critic, is a group of musicians who for some unknown, deeply grating reason, have been stationed at the back of the stage.
For an actress who has always eschewed vanity, Lear has clearly provided a prize worth relishing—for her and for us.
To sum up, this is indeed a not to be missed star turn by Jackson, with enough positive assets to overcome the directorial missteps.
Several elements of the production distract us from the devastation of that world, by adding distractingly fascinating sign language.
Conceptually, I see where Gold is going but as executed it comes off as amateurish.
Too bad that her frisky, wholly original performance seems to be going head-to-head with a director intent on imposing conceptual devices at every turn.
Jackson's performance is superb — at first.
Glenda Jackson was great fun, but, really, Lear shouldn't be great fun.
If you’re there to see Jackson, you won’t be disappointed.
Without Lear at the center, the production fails to cohere into a well-defined whole and becomes a long three-and-a-half hour trek without a fulfilling payoff.
But Gold’s listless production keeps dragging just when it should be gaining momentum.
What we've got instead, despite the impressive ensemble assembled here, is a bit of a mess.
The new Broadway production of King Lear is a gripping presentation of a classic, with stellar performances by a formidable star and cast and assertive immediacy in its direction and design.
If Jackson’s performance turns this inventive but imperfect production into a must-see of the Broadway Spring season, it’s not just because of her impressive stamina and control.
Watching her unspool and battle against storms both natural and human are delectable.

Gold and Jackson have fashioned something rare: a gut-wrenching show that plays comparatively straight with that insanely daunting, logic-challenging text while taking risks that inevitably will offend purists.
But for audiences, the journey getting to those final moments is a just a little more kick-back enjoyable than usual.
Jackson lives up to expectations, with a powerful, remarkable performance
But you’ll likely feel like a fool if you don’t.
Go for Ms. Jackson, bewilder at the rest.
This 'King Lear' is a polished crown that could use a few more thorns.

"The dominant color in Lear's court is gold; a porcelain bulldog and lion straddle the throne. These choices, with their whiff of Art Deco, are no doubt topical, though never fully explored: the text, about the dissolution of ancient Britain, doesn't really speak to our current political moment, and that's okay.
Glenda Jackson was great fun, but, really, Lear shouldn't be great fun.
But Shakespeare’s King Lear requires an unflinching, messy exposure of guts, and pain, and Jackson isn’t willing to do that.

Glenda Jackson in Sam Gold's King Lear is never dull but like the uneven production is never memorable except for the wrong reasons.
It’s a muddle of a production because Sam Gold, the director, seems to have thrown every idea he’s ever had at it and then left the room.
The befuddling King Lear is, to put it bluntly, a hot mess.

"Her characterization in the current production is a dismayingly small-scale creation, stripped of grandeur and only rarely making meaningful contact with the others onstage. Indeed, this Lear barely seems to be a king at all...The rest of Sam Gold's production is a mix of interesting and irritating ideas...
At the end, as the deaths and gimmicks pile up around King Lear, it’s impossible not to view the proceedings as a showcase for anything but the play.
Overall, this production is a sorry mess and cannot be recommended.
It gives me no joy to report that Jackson and the production are both superficial, incoherent and emotionally dead.
